column2: Has the government erected or contributed to the erection of a bait' freezer establishment at Canso, N.S., upon property which is not owned by or vested in the Crown ?

In what work was such steamer engaged after ceasing to be employed in connection with the herring industry ?

column2: Yes.

The plant is to be operated under regulations sanctioned by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and a representative of the department at Ottawa shall be on the board of directors.

column1: The paid-up capital of the company shall not be less than $60,000.
No mortgage shall be placed on the building or plant without the sanction of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
Bait shall be sold to bank fishermen and boat fishermen at the current market rate, and Canadian boats and vessels shall be given a rebate of 10 per cent on the current market rate.
The freezer is to be operated to the fullest extent for at least fifteen years after the expiration of the bonus.
Failing the fulfilment of any of these conditions, the building and plant is to revert to His Majesty.

column2: Information was obtained by the herring drifting operations respecting the movements and resorts of the herring schools offshore, which information has hitherto been very imperfect.

column1: The superior quality of Canadian herring for curing purposes, after the Scottish methods, has been established beyond question.

New and highly remunerative markets have been practically opened by the sample shipments of Scotch cured herring from Canso, which were pronounced by New York buyers to be equal to the best Scotch or Norwegian herring.

Such widespread interest has been created amongst the herring fishermen all along our Atlantic shores that, by the continuation of the experiment for a longer period, a general and immediate improvement of Canadian cured herring is inevitable.

column1: 165585,ca.proc.d.1905-02-16.7.2,1905-02-16,unmatched,,,,GLENN ROSS POST OFFICE.,,,"1.
column2: From die 1st December, 1882.

This office was closed owing to the fact that the postmaster resigned and almost immediately afterwards left the locality. The retiring postmaster expressed the opinion that nobody was willing to accept the office, and, as he pressed to be relieved at once, the inspector decided that he had no recourse but to close it.
The office was re-opened on the 1st November, 1904.

LEFURGEY.,,PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND MAID SERVICE,,,Would the lion., the Postmaster General give us some information as to the condition of the mail service to and from Prince Edward Island at present ? There are only four boats available to cross each way, and the mails are piled up on either side to such an extent

that it is impossible to handle them. A great part of the mails have been transferred from the Straits to the steamer ' Minto ' and will probably be lying on that boat until the end of March unless we get much milder weather than has prevailed this last month. The ' Minto ' and the * Stanley ' have been tied up since the 24th of January and are likely to be tied up another month. I understand that the service at the Capes has not been such as should have been provided to meet an emergency of this kind. I have reliable information that in one case when there was a boat available in the boat house at the Capes, they had to telegraph to Ottawa for permission to get it out and and have it manned and it took three days before they could get an order from Ottawa. When the department are aware that the steamers are tied up, they should use every effort to have a sufficient force put on the other boats available to carry the mails across. The people on the Island have had no newspapers and very few letters since the 4th of the month. During the space of 16 days, there was only one mail. Moncton, N.B., Feb. 16th, 1905.
D. Pottinger, Ottawa.

Another heavy snow storm with high north east wind commenced early this a.m., and extends all east of Bathurst. Number 34, one hour and a half late. Number 9 arrived St. John two hours late. 165633,ca.proc.d.1905-02-16.19.2,1905-02-16,4377f02c-8021-4cd3-9d64-deaad7b31431,ca.m.6238,Mr. W. F. COCKSHUTT (Brantford).,,INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.,,,"I had hoped that the minister would make some report of his consideration of this clause since our last debate upon the Bill. Before entering again upon the discussion of this clause, I desire to call the attention of the House to a statement that appeared in one of our leading newspapers with regard to what I said of this clause on that occasion. I refer to a statement that appeared in the Toronto ' Globe ' of February 1, representing me as saying that I desired the farmers of my district to be brought under the operation of the Act. I wish to state that that is a gross misrepresentation of what I said. I asked for no special favours for the farmers of my district, nor did I ask that any restrictions should be placed upon the farmers of my district that were not equally placed upon the farmers of the whole Dominion. This was a very unfair and a gross misrepresentation of the remarks I made on that occasion. I was discussing the Bill with the desire of making it as perfect as possible, and was offering the minister the suggestions I had to make as one engaged in the business. I was not considering how it might affect my district when the next vote came on, but addressed myself to the question simply with a view to making practical and useful suggestions. I think it is not right that such misrepresentations should be made.

I do not take back anything I said on that occasion, in spite of the misrepresentations. Since the last debate on the Bill, a large deputation waited on the Minister of Agriculture; and I think he will agree with me that it carried weight. There were practical men there who have spent their lives in the study of this great question. There were men there with technical knowledge such as few of those on the floor of this House or either side possess. These men gave their best energies for two hours and a half to lay before the minister the points on which they thought this Bill would conflict with the best interests of trade and agriculture. The minister knows what took place on that occasion, so it is unnecessary to advise him. I wish to say here, what appeared very evident on that occasion, that the Bill, if it has a principle at all is the supply of seeds of purity to the farmers and growers of the country. But, having declared that principle, the Bill proceeds at once to throw down the fence it has raised. The Bill hedges the trade about with restrictions-they shall only sell seeds of purity-and then, in a later clause it throws the whole thing open so that every grower Sir WILFRID LAURIER.

and every farmer may sell these seeds to his neighbours irrespective of any law. I took issue with that on the occasion of the last debate, and I stand by that still. If our object is to assert the principle of pure seed, it is absurd to make such a distinction in the selling of seeds that what will be a criminal act on the part of one man will be perfectly justifiable on the part of another. Not only is this a violation of the principle laid down in the Bill, but it is class legislation that, in my opinion, this country is not prepared for. I say there are many very good reasons why this clause should apply to the grower. I would like the minister to state here to-day why a dealer might not be a grower also; and if I, as a dealer, become a farmer and grower, shall I be free to sell from my barn seeds that I am prohibited from selling from my warehouse? That would appear to be the case under the Bill as it is framed. The minister permits the sale of seeds from a barn, storehouse or granary that would be prohibited if from a store. This is plainly class legislation. Further, I contend it is not in the interest of the farmers themselves. It is universally admitted by agriculturists, I think, that seeds should be planted in a different district from that in which they are grown. The interchange of seed by immediate neighbours is not a good thing. It is better by far to bring your seed from a distance than to buy it from your next-door neighbour. Now, I do not know whether the minister is aware or not, but I am aware, that some farmers are not only growers but dealers also. I could give him the names of farmers in my own district who not only grow seed of their own but also buy from their neighbours.

They have got a name for handling seeds well, they are good cleaners, they grow it well, and they have a name of buying a good class of seeds. These men not only grow their seeds themselves, but they buy seeds from their neighbours' fields. Though this Bill says the seed should be grown upon their land, what is there in the Bill to show that the seed that is sold from a barn is grown upon the farm in which that barn stands ? Who is to see to that ? Does he see the farm ? The farmer may have a show field in front of his premises growing fine seed, so that all the neighbours will say, pee that beautiful clean field. Though he might sell the product of a hundred acres from his barn-there is nothing here to prohibit him from doing that, and there is no, thing here to prevent him from selling seed that he has obtained from some other source than his own growing. He may do that. Therefore, I submit that that clause is not ia the interest of the dealer, it is not in the interest of the farmer himself and it is not in the interest of the grower. If the minister will examine that point carefully, I think he will see his way to alter that clause.

Further, I desire to point out what I pointed out on a previous occasion, that it is impossible-I make that statement deliberately-to placard every bag, receptacle or package with all the names there designated. Further, there is nothing to limit the size of the bag, receptacle or package. A receptacle, under the clause, so far as I can read it, may contain a thousand bushels of seed, it may be a large bin in which there may be a thousand bushels of seed. If that seed is not right, the man may be fined $5, but if he proceeds to put that thousand bushels into a thousand separate bags, he immediately becomes responsible for a thousand times that fine. Why should the quantity affect the fine ? He may put this into smaller packages still. When I raised the point the other day the minister said I had in mind ten cent packages. Not at all. Grass seeds are always put up in sacks. Let me refer to the white, Dutch clover. That is sold very generally by druggists, almost in every town and city, it is used in towns and cities almost entirely. It is impossible to placard that small bag containing five or ten pounds with all these names. Further, having placarded those bags with all these names, it becomes necessary not only to placard the bag with the names of the weeds contained therein, but also the seed that is sold. Now I wish to remind the minister that there is a very large amount of valuable seed that is grown in a mingled state. ;I cannot find in this clause or in any other clause that provision is made for handling that class of seed. It is not uncommon that in the same field there may be red clover, alsike clover and timothy seed, all grown in the one field, all nearly pure ; and still under the Act I do not find that the minister makes provision for the handling of these seeds, which every one knows are perfectly legitimate articles of trade. In fact the farmer in buying them often brings one sack to contain the three lots, and takes them all home in the one bag, they having been mixed in his presence. Surely it does not appear that the minister has given that consideration to this clause that he should have done. I contend that it is desirable to put practical and workable legislation on our statute-books,, and I say that if this clause goes through as it is it will do a great wrong. It throws down the principle that has been laid down regarding the purity of the seed. It permits one man to deal in an article that it condemns another man for handling, and it opens the door for the minister to allow the sale from one premise of an article that he would not allow to be sold from another. That is a system of legislation we are not ready for. It is going to do great harm, not only to the agriculturist, but also to the dealer and all concerned in the trade.
I asked a question the other day, which was answered, I regret to say, in my absence. the answer showing the various coun-37$

tries to which these seeds referred to are exported. I notice there is a list of thirteen countries to which these seeds are exported. That is in spite of the fact that we have no law at present governing seeds. We sell thousands of bushels of seeds to the very best countries, to men who are well acquainted with seeds. We will be prohibited to a large extent from doing that, because we will be compelled to label them with the names of certain weeds. I wish to point out to the Minister that under his Act he does not recognize the standards that rule in the trade at all. On the next clause, perhaps, I may more fully touch upon the point I refer to now, and that is with regard to the test which he submits the seed to. lie submits it to a test with regard to purity and germination. Now purity and germination are only partial tests of the value of seeds, as any one knows who is engaged in the trade, but a comparatively small part of the test. You may have a perfectly pure seed but very weak. It may germinate, but it will be very weak. It may be a seed that is not matured, it may be perfectly pure of its kind, but it is only about half size. Now to have a No. 1 seed you must have a seed that is fully developed, and it must not only be fully developed in size, but well developed in colour. Any man who handles seeds will tell you that those are the requisites that go to make up a first-class sample of seed. After the minister has laid down his law as to what constitutes a first-class seed, he has not got a first-class seed at all-not nearly as good as is sold tc-day under a less high grade than he proposes to establish here, for the reason that it may be perfect in purity and germination, but it is deficient in size and colour, two of the requisites of a first-class seed. I do not like to refer the minister to anything so small as small potatoes, but I can show him perhaps, just what I mean. You take five bushels of potatoes and cull from them one bushel of small size, only fit for hog feed. You give those to the hogs, and probably that is the best end of them. But these potatoes you culled out were, according to the minister's test, pure of their kind and would germinate. Now both of these points are fully established, they are pure and will germinate, and still they are *tery far short of what they should be according to the standard set up. Therefore, I contend that the minister is not laying down a proper law in endeavouring to force us to label a seed if it has got ten weed seeds to a thousand good seeds. It may be possible to have ten weed seeds to a thousand, and still be a far better article than we will have under this Bill. Any one that knows the state of the trade, knows that is a fact. Why should we be compelled to brand that package with all the imperfections in it ? Who would be able to sell a horse if he were obliged to brand all the imperfections on that horse ? Who would

be able to sell any article under those conditions ? Yet the hon. gentleman asks the seedsmen to brand upon their package every impurity and every imperfection, and then says, buy it if you dare. It is not a fair way of doing business, it is not a right way, it is not a way that will commend itself; I believe, to the intelligence of this country and this House.

Further, it is calculated to do an immense amount of damage to trade that ha3 been established. I say that this trade haS been well established under great difficulties. 165656,ca.proc.d.1905-02-16.19.25,1905-02-16,8898cbb9-c7b4-4b1d-8019-f6672fcd0560,ca.m.110,Mr. FISHER.,Minister of Agriculture,INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.,,,If he does not do so, it is presumed that it is because he is satisfied of the quality of the seed he is getting. If he feels any doubt about the seed he is getting, he can require that the transaction shall be brought under the action of the law. If he knows enough about the farmer and the seed he need not do so. The reason, however, for this exemption is that the grower of the seed himself, the farmer, has practically no way of knowing what the seedsman, who is in the business and who does as a matter of fact clean seed and who has machinery for cleaning seed, can easily know, but which the farmer selling as he does on his own premises seed which he grew himself would find it very difficult indeed if at all possible to know. This Bill provides especially for the sale of cereals where in small transactions between neighbours seed may be sold and not be subject to the provisions of this section of the law.

I want to point out further that this exemption applies only to one section of the law. It does not allow the farmer to mark his; seeds as first quality. It only exempts him from the necessity of putting upon them the name of certain weeds, for the reason that he cannot and ought not to be expected to know the seeds of weeds in the way that a dealer or seedsman would know them. The intention of the section is to

permit of transactions between neighbours such as are common in all sections of the country. The farmer at one season may be out of clover seed or grass seed, or he may want a little oats or wheat or barley to sow his fields with, and he is to be allowed to go to his neighbour to get them. He knows his neignbour's fields and method of farming, and may, therefore, be supposed to be able to judge fairly well of the quality of the seeds he is buying. If he chooses to risk buying them without bringing the transaction under the operation of the Act, he can do so, but if he wishes to protect himself he can demand that the transaction shall be brought under the operation of the Act, and then it shall be subject to all the penalties and restrictions which the Act provides. It seems to me that we should not interfere with transactions of that kind. Interference would not only be unnecessary, but it would be unfair ami would create a hardship in the business of agriculture. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt) has referred to this as a means of selling bad seeds. I do not think it is. I do not think it will produce the same kind of difficulty in the seed trade that the sale of bad seeds by seedsmen or dealers would do ; because this sale of seeds would not spread the weeds which may be contained in them over a large area of country. My hon. friend from Grey said a few minutes ago that he had known men to go sixty miles for seeds. That is a pretty long distance, I should think about the limit of the distance that could come under the operation of this clause. But a seedsman may sell seeds in another province, to some one a thousand miles away. Nobody knows whether he is going to sell seeds to be used on the next farm or at a great distance. The origin of the seed is quite out of reach of the knowledge of the purchaser. As a matter of fact, I do not think the seedsmen themselves, when they fill an order, can generally tell where the seeds came from. 1 may say that when this subclause was first drawn it was not even limited to the sale of seeds by a farmer on his premises. If a farmer sold seed to another person, to be used for seeding, he was to be allowed to do so. I think I have hedged this exemption round with every possible limitation which could be introduced without creating a very great hardship and hinder-ance to the agricultural operations of farmers, and I do not see how it is possible for me to go any further in that respect. When representations were made to me the other day by the deputation of seedsmen, I told them that I would be glad to consider what they proposed, and all they proposed was that the effect of the certificate should be reversed, that is to say, that the sale should come under the operations of the Act, unless the seller required a certificate from the purchaser. One would Imagine, from what the hon. member from Brantford

has said, that the deputation had deliberately asked for the elimination of this clause altogether. They said that they would be glad to have it eliminated, but finally, when the matter simmered down, the amount of their request in the end was as I have said that we should reverse the certificate. I feel that I cannot go as far as that and that I must ask the committee to adopt the clause as it stands in the Bill.

Any such inspector may, during the day time, enter any store, shop, warehouse, mill, elevator or other premises occupied by any person who vends grain, grass or other seed for feed or seeding purposes, and may inspect such seeds or grain to ascertain if they contain any seeds of noxious weeds, and may take away a

165721,ca.proc.d.1905-02-16.19.90,1905-02-16,80f4de9d-1b1a-4db1-93cf-9cb7b9b63dd4,ca.m.9843,Mr. CARYELL.,,INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.,,,I have listened to'the discussion this afternoon on this question, and, while not a practical farmer, I represent a farming constituency, and I have observed that the discussion has been nearly altogether from the standpoint of the seed merchant and to some extent from the standpoint of the province of Ontario. I have heard two or three speeches from gentlemen from the west, but not a word as yet from the maritime provinces. I would therefore like to discuss this measure for a few moments from the standpoint of a maritime member, and one of the representatives of the maritime farmers. I can assure you that there is no question of so much importance to the maritime farmers to-day as the seed question. We have attempted for some years to improve the quality of the seeds we have to use. We cannot tell why, but it is a fact that we do not raise our own grass seeds to any great extent in the maritime provinces. We are compelled to purchase them mostly from the province of Ontario, and it seems almost impossible for a farmer to get a good quality of grass seeds. He can prepare his land for a crop of wheat or any other grain, and the crop will be fairly free from weeds ; but the next year after he uses Ontario grass seed, he will probably have more sorrel in his crop than timothy or clover. Our farmers have taken various courses in their efforts to overcome this difficulty. They have banded themselves together in societies and have imported the seed direct; our merchants have tried to get good seed for them ; but no matter what we do, it seems impossible to get good results, Now, it seems to me that this Bill is exactly in the right direction. It has been described here this afternoon, I think by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt), as a drastic measure ; I think he almost: went so far as to say it was vicious legislation, and he did say that it was

legislation unprecedented in the annals of any civilized country. Well, Sir, if this Bill *will be the means of overcoming some of the difficulties under which the farmers of this country are suffering in connection with the purchase of their grass seed, then Canada will have the distinction of being the first civilized country which has tried to grapple with this question. I cannot see any difficulty in the way of working it out. It seems to me that it, would be nonsense to appoint a staff of inspectors to enforce the Act. If it is going to be useful to the farmers, they will find the means of working it out. If it become law. we in the province of New Brunswick will do so, whether they will in the province of Ontario or not. We will simply get some farmer to take a sample of the grass seed which he has purchased from his local merchant, and have it tested, and if it does not come up to the requirements, we will lay an information against the local merchant and see where the trouble is. You may say that this will be a hardship on an innocent merchant. By no means, because by subsection 2 of section S, if the merchant be able to show that the package has not been broken, and that he has purchased it in good faith, and gives the name of the merchant in Montreal or Toronto from whom he has bought the seed, the onus will fall back upon the latter.

Then, as I have said, it is estimated that $140,000 will be required to complete the work, of which we are now

asking $80,000. I wish to correct a statement I made a few moments ago. X was asked as to deepening rock cut on the Welland canal and as to the contract price for the earth excavation. There was no earth excavation provided for in the contract; it was all rock cutting and the lowest tender was $2.90 per cubic yard. The earth work I had in mind at the moment was deepening portions of the summit level, the contract price for which is 38Jc. per cubic yard. 166102,ca.proc.d.1905-02-16.20.6.167,1905-02-16,05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae,ca.m.1687,Mr. EMMERSON.,Minister of Railways and Canals,SUPPLY.,,,It is necessary in connection with this vote under the law of Ontario to employ a regularly qualified land surveyor-hon. gentlemen from Ontario will know whether that' is correct or not- in fixing bounds which may be in dispute.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Samuel Barker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=8aa5c0ed-bcaa-4229-9464-8fbd967acc30&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL
166105,ca.proc.d.1905-02-16.20.6.170,1905-02-16,8aa5c0ed-bcaa-4229-9464-8fbd967acc30,ca.m.645,Mr. BARKER.,,SUPPLY.,,,Every man of that class who has been taken from Ontario is probably a provincial land surveyor.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Samuel Barker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=8aa5c0ed-bcaa-4229-9464-8fbd967acc30&Language=E&Section=ALL
166106,ca.proc.d.1905-02-16.20.6.171,1905-02-16,05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae,ca.m.1687,Mr. EMMERSON.,Minister of Railways and Canals,SUPPLY.,,,I am not aware of it. If it is so it would cover the difficulty but the chief engineer tells me that he thinks that they are not.

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL
166107,ca.proc.d.1905-02-16.20.6.172,1905-02-16,5bfd2fe5-bfe6-42c4-9503-71c3b6f865df,ca.m.5370,Mr. LENNOX.,,SUPPLY.,,,There is another aspect of the case that X would like to call the hon. minister's attention to and it is this; assuming that there is a dispute between a landowner and the government in what way does the hon. minister propose to adjust It ? Ordinarily in a case of dispute between adjoining owners each party pays a portion of the costs. How does the government propose to do it ? If these parties are claiming that they are entitled to land which has been and is in the possession of the government, and it seems to me that the government is now fairly in possession, it is for these parties who are claiming the land to establish their title to it, or at all events, to pay a portion of the expense. Why the government should take upon itself to make a survey of the whole line for that purpose and expend a matter of $20,000, I cannot understand. Does the hon. minister apprehend the point I am speaking of ? It is that in any dispute between adjoining owners the person who is not in possession and who is claiming to obtain possession from the other is the person who enters the proceedings and it will be for the land-owner to have the limits marked out on the ground according to the provisions of the deed defining the boundaries.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Haughton Lennox,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=5bfd2fe5-bfe6-42c4-9503-71c3b6f865df&Language=E&Section=ALL
166108,ca.proc.d.1905-02-16.20.6.173,1905-02-16,05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae,ca.m.1687,Mr. EMMERSON.,Minister of Railways and Canals,SUPPLY.,,,In a mere delimitation of bounds that may be correct, but there is other work to be done in connection with this-the preparation of the plans and the fixing of the monuments. I do not think that the parties holding the adjacent properties will be bound in any way to contribute to that. It would not be so necessary to them and I think it is more important for the government to have these bounds fixed because the present state of affairs opens the door to constant claims being pressed. The people are not so much interested in that as the government is.

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL
166109,ca.proc.d.1905-02-16.20.6.174,1905-02-16,5bfd2fe5-bfe6-42c4-9503-71c3b6f865df,ca.m.5370,Mr. LENNOX.,,SUPPLY.,,,I cannot see that the hon. minister has made it very clear yet as to the .position we are in in reference to this matter. We have been in possession of the canal for years and years. We must have been using it. We are using the land. In the majority of instances I assume that the adjoining owners along the canal are using their lands. There will be fences in many instances, probably in almost all instances, and in regard to the plan that my hon. friend speaks of, the plan follows the survey ; it does not precede it. You make the survey and then you prepare the plan, I presume. If the hon. minister will tell us how this $20,000 is made up, probably it will be satisfactory, but we have no information as yet on that point. There will be so much time involved, so much for the plan and so on. Will the hon. minister tell us that ?

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Haughton Lennox,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=5bfd2fe5-bfe6-42c4-9503-71c3b6f865df&Language=E&Section=ALL
166110,ca.proc.d.1905-02-16.20.6.175,1905-02-16,05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae,ca.m.1687,Mr. EMMERSON.,Minister of Railways and Canals,SUPPLY.,,,I have no details of the estimate. The officers have not furnished me with them. I am acting on the estimate prepared for me by the chief engineer of canals and he concluded that this work would cost $20,000. We are asking a vote for that amount. I do not think it is an excessive amount. It cannot exceed that amount because that is the only amount provided, but if it does not cost that amount the whole of it would certainly not be expended.

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL
166111,ca.proc.d.1905-02-16.20.6.176,1905-02-16,5bfd2fe5-bfe6-42c4-9503-71c3b6f865df,ca.m.5370,Mr. LENNOX.,,SUPPLY.,,,I do not know whether I quite comprehend what the hon. minister means when he speaks of the estimate. What I understand by an estimate is that a person sits down and takes into consideration the various elements that enter into the various kinds of work and so on, and having set down the figures in detail he then finds out what the total will be. I do not understand that an estimate is a mere guess as the hon. minister says it is. It is simply that the deputy minister instructs him to put down $20,000 and down it goes. He says it may not be expended, but our experience is that when we vote money it is expended, and very often more than expended. We ought to have something more than a mere guess. We ought to have some figures to show how this amount is arrived at. If the hon. minister has such figures he ought to bring them down and if he has not he ought not to ask us to vote this amount until these figures are prepared.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Haughton Lennox,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=5bfd2fe5-bfe6-42c4-9503-71c3b6f865df&Language=E&Section=ALL
166112,ca.proc.d.1905-02-16.20.6.177,1905-02-16,74dd6652-cc90-4645-97e9-bfadb4e237e7,ca.m.6207,Mr. HENDERSON.,,SUPPLY.,,,I would like to ask the hon. minister when this work will likely be completed. Will it be done during next summer or will it extend over several years ? It may be that $20,000 is only the thin end of the wedge, only a very small part of the expense necessary. We seem to have a great many of these continuous jobs running on year after year extending over two, three, four, five, or six years. There must be a great many people in this country very happy with such contracts. They seem to make their living out of them. They never seem to come to any termination. This is a policy that we will have to inquire into. Probably this survey bureau to survey the Welland canal is another of these never ending contracts. I would not be surprised if those of us who are here three or four years hence will .still be voting money for the survey of the Welland canal.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,David Henderson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=74dd6652-cc90-4645-97e9-bfadb4e237e7&Language=E&Section=ALL

This is only the estimate of the chief engineer. This work has become urgent. The work should be done at once and as I am informed by the chief engineer it will be commenced as soon as the vote is available and will be completed certainly within the fiscal year commencing the first of July next. The reason why it is urgent that the work should be done is that in one instance, it is

claimed by the engineers, the bounds of the canal go right through the barn and house of one of the adjoining owners. It is claimed by the department that this man has encroached on the property of the canal by erecting his buildings there.

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL
166114,ca.proc.d.1905-02-16.20.6.179,1905-02-16,8aa5c0ed-bcaa-4229-9464-8fbd967acc30,ca.m.645,Mr. BARKER.,,SUPPLY.,,,You can ascertain that for $10.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Samuel Barker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=8aa5c0ed-bcaa-4229-9464-8fbd967acc30&Language=E&Section=ALL

I think it will be necessary to make a complete survey of the whole line in order to ascertain with certainty where the monuments should be placed.

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Edward Cochrane,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a8b48423-a177-428b-932c-de0c479bc9de&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL

It is absurd for intelligent men to be sitting here in parliament voting away the people's money and laughing and thinking they are so clever. Minister of Railways and Canals as to the necessity of having fuller information about his estimates. I understand that the Minister of Railways and Canals is a little new here, but the Minister of Customs knows how, when he was in opposition he used to howl about these expenditures.

,Liberal,,William Mulock,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=3fbbf99b-cf52-4821-bdc6-2ec9565a294a&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Liberal,,William Mulock,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=3fbbf99b-cf52-4821-bdc6-2ec9565a294a&Language=E&Section=ALL
